meta.title: Who really said "She Runs the Gamut of Human Emotion from A to B"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Dorothy Parker really did make the joke — she said so herself. But the famous wording is a columnist’s, and the target was Katharine Hepburn on stage, not on film.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'She Runs the Gamut of Human Emotion from A to B'?
meta.ogDescription: Parker admitted the A-to-B crack was hers. The wording everybody quotes, though, came from Walter Winchell’s column six months later.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic and Algonquin Round Table wit
answer.sourceLine: Parker made the joke about Katharine Hepburn in The Lake over the winter of 1933–34, and admitted as much years later: asked about it by Garson Kanin she said, “Oh, I said it all right.” What she never did was write it down. Every surviving 1934 printing is somebody else reporting her, and each one words it differently — so the exact sentence quoted today cannot be pinned to Parker’s own pen.

source.excerpt: “Come,” she said, “let’s all go to see Miss Hepburn and hear her run the gamut of emotions from A to B!”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the barb to a New York Sun column of 6 January 1934 and concludes that it “has been ascribed to Dorothy Parker and there is substantive evidence supporting the ascription” — while noting that the earliest 1930s evidence is not from Parker directly and appears to be thirdhand.

Parker confirmed it herself. Quote Investigator quotes Garson Kanin’s Tracy and Hepburn (1971): asked “But what about ‘all the way from A to B’?” she answered, “Oh, I said it all right. You know how it is. A joke.” ↗

Wikiquote ↗ files the line among Parker’s sourced quotations by way of Alexander Woollcott’s essay “Our Mrs Parker” in While Rome Burns (1934), where it reads “Miss Hepburn, it seems, had run the whole gamut from A to B” — and records that the words do not appear in a printed Parker review but “were elsewhere described as a spoken remark.”

The occasion is documented: Wikipedia ↗ dates Hepburn’s The Lake to a Broadway run opening 26 December 1933 at the Martin Beck Theatre. That is a stage play, which is why the Reader’s Digest version placing the quip in a review of the film Little Women disagrees with every earlier report.
source.excerptNote: The earliest printing Quote Investigator located, in John S. Cohen Jr.’s New York Sun column of 6 January 1934. Note that it is not the sentence people quote: Time made it “human emotion,” Alexander Woollcott made it “the whole gamut,” and Walter Winchell’s June 1934 column produced the wording that stuck.

source.rightsNote: The remark was spoken over the winter of 1933–34 and first appeared in print on 6 January 1934. United States copyright can reach works first published from 1931 onward, so nothing here falls into the pre-1931 public domain, and we have classified it conservatively. Two honest caveats: a single spoken sentence this short may not attract copyright at all, and we did not check the renewal status of the 1934 periodicals that carried it.

author.name: Dorothy Parker
author.heading: About Dorothy Parker
author.metaLine: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic and short-story writer; founding wit of the Algonquin Round Table
author.bio: Dorothy Parker made her name as a theatre critic for Vanity Fair and a book reviewer for The New Yorker, where she wrote as Constant Reader. She was the most quotable member of the Algonquin Round Table, which is both her fame and her problem: the table’s reputation for wit made her a magnet for other people’s jokes, and Wikiquote now carries a longer list of things she did not say than most authors have quotations. She later wrote for Hollywood, was twice nominated for an Academy Award for screenwriting, and was blacklisted for her left-wing politics.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: Nobody seriously doubts that Parker made the joke. What travels with it — an older author, a different occasion, and a sentence she never uttered — is another matter, and the arguments started within weeks.

items.who: “She runs the gamut of human emotion from A to B”
items.why: This exact sentence first appears in Walter Winchell’s column in the Syracuse Journal of 9 June 1934, roughly six months after the remark was made, and it is the version that stuck. The earliest printing, in January 1934, has Parker saying “let’s all go to see Miss Hepburn and hear her run the gamut of emotions from A to B” — and Quote Investigator ↗ records at least five further wordings in 1934 alone.

Reader’s Digest printed the joke in May 1934 as “Reviewing the motion picture, Little Women, Dorothy Parker writes of Katherine Hepburn’s acting…”, per Quote Investigator ↗. The earlier reports all place the remark at The Lake, a Broadway play, and describe it as something Parker said aloud rather than wrote.

On 24 February 1934 the columnist O. O. McIntyre complained that the line “was fresher when William Winter, a gentler critic, pulled it on an actress of 30 years ago… Most Algonquin gags are that way,” as Quote Investigator ↗ reproduces. No earlier Winter text carrying the joke has been produced.

Quote Investigator records that in June 1934 Walter Winchell was told by the humorist Irvin S. Cobb that the quip went “all the way back to Jonathan Swift” ↗. No such passage in Swift has been located.

misattribution.truthLine: The joke is Parker’s, by her own admission to Garson Kanin. The sentence you have read is a newspaper columnist’s tidying-up of it, and the victim was Katharine Hepburn on a Broadway stage, not on a screen.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The Lake was meant to be Katharine Hepburn’s Broadway vindication after Hollywood had made her famous. It opened at the Martin Beck the day after Christmas 1933 and closed some six weeks later, and Parker’s eleven-word demolition outlived the production by nearly a century.

The joke works because of what it withholds. It does not say the performance was bad; it says it was narrow — two adjacent letters out of twenty-six — and lets the reader do the arithmetic. That compression is exactly what Alexander Woollcott admired in it when he put it into While Rome Burns the same year.
detailsBody: The remark’s survival is a case study in how a spoken joke becomes a quotation. Nobody wrote it down at the time; five different journalists reported it from hearsay within six months, each smoothing it a little, and the version that won was not the first but the catchiest.

Hepburn herself came to terms with it. She was 26 when the notice landed — born in May 1907 ↗ — and went on to a record four Academy Awards for Best Actress; the barb is now told as an anecdote about her early stage career rather than a verdict on it. Quote Investigator ends its own article on that note — “perceptions are labile, and Hepburn went on to a magnificent career.”
context.pull: Two letters out of twenty-six, and the reader does the rest.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest known printing is the New York Sun, 6 January 1934, John S. Cohen Jr., "The Talking Pictures," p. 9 col. 1, reading "let’s all go to see Miss Hepburn and hear her run the gamut of emotions from A to B!"
Parker confirmed the joke to Garson Kanin ("Oh, I said it all right. You know how it is. A joke.") in Tracy and Hepburn (1971).
Walter Winchell’s Syracuse Journal column of 9 June 1934 carries the wording "She runs the gamut of human emotion from A to B".
Reader’s Digest, May 1934, placed the joke in a review of the motion picture Little Women.
O. O. McIntyre, 24 February 1934, claimed the joke was older and credited it to the critic William Winter.
Wikiquote lists the line under Woollcott’s "Our Mrs Parker" and states the words do not appear in a printed Parker review but were described as a spoken remark.
The Lake opened 26 December 1933 at the Martin Beck Theatre starring Katharine Hepburn and closed in February 1934.
The Internet Archive holds a 1934 edition of Alexander Woollcott’s While Rome Burns.

Dorothy Parker lived 22 August 1893 to 7 June 1967, wrote theatre criticism for Vanity Fair from 1918, reviewed books for The New Yorker as “Constant Reader” between 1927 and 1933, received two Academy Award screenwriting nominations, was placed on the Hollywood blacklist, and was a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table.
Katharine Hepburn was born 12 May 1907 and won a record four Academy Awards for Best Actress.
